fixes.explanation: I get why this feels true, since watchmen are the ones guarding the city. But Solomon, Israel's king, says "unless the LORD protects the city, its watchmen stand guard in vain." The guarding isn't the thing that makes the city safe. The LORD protecting it is.

"…for He gives sleep to His beloved." That's the end of verse 2. Solomon, Israel's king, says rising early and staying up late, toiling for bread to eat, is in vain, and then he names what He gives to His beloved: sleep. A whole verse about working, and it lands on a pillow.

Land is a solid guess, but it's not in this verse. The line says "…He gives sleep to His beloved." Solomon, Israel's king, puts that right alongside rising early and staying up late. No deed to the property, just sleep.
"Children are indeed a heritage from the LORD…" That's how verse 3 begins. A heritage is something handed to you. The psalm says the LORD is the One handing it.
Solomon's name is on this psalm, so the king is an easy guess. But Solomon, Israel's king, points somewhere else. He says "Children are indeed a heritage from the LORD…" The credit goes to the LORD.

Standing before a king would make anybody nervous. But the psalm doesn't mention a king here. It says the man "…will not be put to shame when he confronts the enemies at the gate." The setting is the gate.
Verse 2 says "For when you eat the fruit of your labor, blessings and prosperity will be yours." It's a gift that comes with the work. Blessings and prosperity, fresh out of the oven if you ask me.

The song says "…your sons like olive shoots sitting around your table." It compares the sons to olive shoots, which are young, new growth, and it has them sitting around the table. It's a picture of a family together.

Olive shoots do make you think of a field, and I understand the guess. But the song says "…your sons like olive shoots sitting around your table." The sons are sitting around the table, not out in a field.

"In this way indeed shall blessing come to the man who fears the LORD." That's verse 4, and it ties up what came before. It starts with "In this way," pointing back at the wife, the sons and the table. The word it lands on is blessing.
Testing is a real part of life, but that's not what this verse says. It says "In this way indeed shall blessing come to the man who fears the LORD." The word is blessing.

The song says "May the LORD bless you from Zion, that you may see the prosperity of Jerusalem all the days of your life…" It's a wish for the whole city's good, not only the family at the table. It starts with "May the LORD bless you from Zion," so it's a wish.

Egypt never comes up in this song. The verse says "…that you may see the prosperity of Jerusalem all the days of your life…" Egypt's riches would make a fancy souvenir, but the song has your eyes on Jerusalem.
